title: The Shutdown Build: Why a Manufacturer's Final Production Run Before Christmas Doesn't Turn Into Cash Until February
linkedin:
A manufacturer running its production line flat out in late November usually feels like good news.

It can also be the exact moment cash quietly leaves the business.

Most manufacturers build a buffer of finished stock before a Christmas shutdown, enough to keep key customers supplied through the weeks the factory is closed. That stock gets paid for in materials, labour and freight well before a single invoice is raised. On standard thirty to sixty day terms, the cash it represents often doesn't land until February.

None of the decisions that create this gap look wrong in isolation. Running the line harder, building the buffer, protecting a key account, each one makes sense on its own.

What catches manufacturers out is that the fixed costs don't pause either. The factory lease, the equipment finance, the insurance, and the staff retained over the break all keep running without a new invoice landing to offset them.

The businesses that move through January calmly are rarely the ones with the quietest shutdown. They're the ones who modelled, back in November, exactly when that last run would turn into cash, and what the January restart would cost before it did.
